text:
I’ll model the fluid volume directly in metres. I interpret each runner as leaving its side wall laterally, continuing straight for 30 mm, then bending downward through 90° on a 60 mm centreline radius; this places the downward-facing port centreline 90 mm laterally from the plenum wall. I’ll place the four runner axes at 37.5, 112.5, 187.5, and 262.5 mm along the 300 mm plenum. The 70 mm throttle passage will be a short 30 mm cylindrical neck at the end; that unstated neck length is an assumption needed to form a distinct inlet patch.

I’ll use a build123d solid union for authoritative CAD and named surface export, then snappyHexMesh from the watertight patch union. First I’m checking the installed API needed for swept tubes and face interrogation.

The installed API supports a solid pipe sweep. I’ll now construct the plenum, throttle neck, and eight runner sweeps, fuse them, print dimensional checks, and export a coarse preview STL. The runners’ circular sections start slightly inside the plenum so the Boolean union has genuine overlap rather than tangent contact.
The sweep path will end exactly 90 mm outboard of each side wall and 60 mm below its start after the quarter-circle bend. I’m building and measuring that coarse CAD now.

The prior cell was rejected by a Python syntax error in a path-evaluation expression, so none of it belongs in the build script. I’ll rerun the construction with the endpoint check taken directly from the defined path coordinates.

The coarse union is one solid with the expected overall envelope: 300 mm plenum length, 30 mm inlet neck, runner outer extent 169 mm from centre due to the 19 mm tube radius, and ports 60 mm below runner axes. I’ll render the coarse preview before assigning faces.

The preview shows the intended single connected manifold volume and all eight unobstructed runner outlets. I’ll now inspect the final solid’s faces by analytic surface type, area, centre, and representative normal. This lets me tag the circular inlet and port faces explicitly by their known construction centres, while assigning runner walls from their cylindrical/toroidal sweep surfaces and the remainder to plenum walls.

The face audit is clean: eight equal circular port faces (area 1,134 mm² each), sixteen analytic runner wall faces (eight straight cylinders plus eight toroidal bends), one circular throttle inlet, and the remaining seven faces are the plenum/end/neck walls. I’ll assign the negative-y bank as `port_left_1..4` and positive-y as `port_right_1..4`, ordered from the throttle end, then export all eleven named patches in one conformal tessellation call.

The exported patch union is watertight and conformal: 69,060 triangles, zero open, flipped, or non-manifold edges. For the coarse mesh I’ll use a 10 mm Cartesian background and one surface refinement level (5 mm near all manifold surfaces), retaining only the connected interior containing `(0.15, 0, 0)`. This gives about 7–8 cells across each 38 mm runner before snapping—appropriate for the requested coarse first pass.
The meshing dictionaries are ready with all eleven STL names carried directly into mesh patches. I’ll generate the background grid and run the coarse snappyHexMesh pass.

snappyHexMesh stopped before meshing because this OpenFOAM release requires minimal `fvSchemes` and `fvSolution` dictionaries even for mesh generation. I’ll add empty valid dictionaries, then rerun both mesh stages in a separate accepted cell so the replayable script does not depend on the failed attempt.
I’ll now rerun `blockMesh` and `snappyHexMesh` from the defined dictionaries.

The runtime dictionaries are now accepted, but snappy found a syntax error in the generated `refinementSurfaces` entries. I’ll inspect the numbered dictionary around the reported line before correcting only that generator.
Each refinement entry has one extra closing brace. I’ll regenerate those entries with balanced patch and entry scopes.
The printed compact form is visually ambiguous, so I’ll have OpenFOAM parse the dictionary with `foamDictionary` before spending another mesh run.
OpenFOAM confirms the entries are still over-closed. I’ll replace the entire `refinementSurfaces` block rather than applying another local textual substitution.

The refinement block now parses; the parser proceeds to a release-specific missing include path for the quality defaults. I’ll locate the installed quality dictionary and either use its actual path or provide the standard required controls explicitly.
OpenFOAM 2512 stores this include as `meshQualityDict.cfg`. I’ll correct the path and validate the whole dictionary before rerunning.
The full dictionary now parses. I’ll rerun both meshing stages and report snappy’s final cell count.

The coarse manifold mesh completed with 19,928 cells. I’ll run the binding bare `checkMesh` and inspect the boundary patch table to ensure all eleven requested names survived and the temporary background patch has no faces.

The binding check passes: one connected region, 19,928 cells, all eleven requested patches, maximum non-orthogonality 42.5°, maximum skewness 1.07, positive cell volumes, and no background boundary faces. The mesh volume is 0.004096 m³ versus CAD volume 0.004123 m³ (0.65% coarse discretisation difference). I’ll now run the completion gate with no waivers; the exported union is expected to be closed, manifold, and consistently wound.
